title: POC weekly fidelity sprint and guardrail pressure test with Kestrel Security
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on fidelity heatmap, guardrail pressure testing, and fallback behavior. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-18 10:00 PT
Duration: 36 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Li (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Eve Robinson (CTO, Kestrel), Derek Huang (Head of MLOps), Sofia Perez (Product), Amir Khan (Security)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync: looked at recent regression spikes after the prompt batch change, did a guardrail pressure test (intent boundary cases), and agreed next steps for stress runs and security scoping.

[00:00] Maya: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining. we have 36 minutes on the clock. quick roll call?
[00:12] Eve: eve here, derek, sofia and amir are on.
[00:15] Derek: yep here.
[00:18] Maya: great. jonah, you want to kick off with the fidelity heatmap findings?
[00:25] Jonah: yeah sure. so from the batch we ran last night, we saw a concentrated regression in the 'credential reset' intent part, about a 6.7% drop in top-1 accuracy when batch size moved from 4 to 12 with the aggressive prompt-ensemble. most of those were prefix-cache misses, so KV cache — or K V cash as the transcriber sometimes says — was a big factor. there were also a handful of hallucination rate upticks on longer context examples.
[00:52] Sofia: are those longer contexts the ones with nested bullets? we saw some user transcripts with like three system messages stacked.
[01:01] Jonah: exactly. the prompt scaffolding we tried was nesting system instructions and user examples to reduce ambiguity but the model variant we used (quantized int8) seems to lose some fidelity on long chain-of-thought style prompts.
[01:15] Derek: can you remind us which model you ran? was it the 13b quant that you mentioned last week?
[01:20] Jonah: correct, 'redwood-13b-qint8-v2' — like we said, it saves token-cost but the attention kernels degrade slightly beyond 2k tokens, especially with our current kernel fallback logic.
[01:33] Amir: security question, does that quantized variant still permit customer-managed KMS for keys used in the private deployment? we need to be explicit for compliance.
[01:42] Lina: yes, on Redwood Private you can still plug in your KMS/HSM. the inference containers talk to the customer-managed KMS for model key wrap; that part isn't changed by quantization.
[01:52] Amir: ok good. is that documented somewhere?
[01:54] Maya: we will send the security integration note — link in the chat — and the SOC2 scope doc.
[02:00] Eve: great. back to fidelity, the heatmap looked worse for financial phrasing in one slice, any idea why?
[02:08] Jonah: that slice had a lot of numeric formatting and currency conversions. the quantized pathways sometimes lose subtle tokenization cues that the float kernels keep. so you'll see scoring drift when the prompt expects exact numeric output.
[02:20] Derek: would switching to fp16 for that slice be an option? we need to know latency cost delta.
[02:25] Jonah: yes, fp16 keeps fidelity but costs ~20% more in GPU time for the same throughput here. we can A/B it: run that slice on fp16 and int8 and compare recall and P95 latency.
[02:36] Maya: action: jonah to run the overnight stress with both variants and update the shared bench sheet.
[02:41] Jonah: noted.
[02:43] [03:00] Maya: next, guardrail pressure testing — we deliberately fed adversarial prompts that try to elicit policy-violating outputs and also ambiguous boundary cases.
[03:12] Sofia: quick interjection, last week's guardrail patch seemed to reduce false positives but increased false negatives in one category.
[03:20] Jonah: yep, the threshold tuning we pushed lowered the safety filter sensitivity to reduce user-facing blocks, but that widened the acceptance window where subtle disallowed content got through. so it's a tradeoff.
[03:31] Amir: for auditability, do you keep per-request policy decision logs? we need tamper-evident audit logs.
[03:38] Lina: yes, we emit policy decisions to the audit stream; for Private deployments those can point to your internal log collector and we support signing if you want tamper-evidence.
[03:47] Amir: ok perfect. so can we get a sample of the decision log format?
[03:50] Maya: we'll attach a sample JSON schema to the ticket.
[03:53] [05:00] Derek: timeline question — if we decide to go Dedicated after POC, what's the expected lead time to get a canary cluster with Kestrel's VPC peering?
[05:10] Maya: for Dedicated, once the contract's in we typically provision in 2-3 weeks for a standard canary region, longer if you require custom on-prem hooks. Private (VPC) is often 3-6 weeks depending on network approvals.
[05:21] Eve: and performance parity between Dedicated and Private? we need predictable SLOs.
[05:26] Jonah: Dedicated and Private run the same serving runtime and kernel selection stack; variance comes from infra differences. we publish per-model perf profiles so you can pick variants that meet your P95 target.
[05:35] [06:00] Sofia: returning to prompts — we tested a prompt-ensemble that shuffles three few-shot examples. the score spread widened, is there a recommended way to prune or re-weight examples?
[06:10] Jonah: yes, we typically do an importance-weighted pruning: score each example contribution via attribution and drop the lowest delta examples or downweight. also try constrained batching so examples that cause KV cache churn don't live in the same request.
[06:22] Derek: that sounds like a lot of engineering on our end. can Redwood help with automated pruning?
[06:26] Maya: Redwood Optimize has a suggestion engine; Jonah can export the signal we collect and run a short auto-prune job.
[06:33] Jonah: I can run a 500-sample auto-prune and share the candidate set.
[06:37] [07:00] Sofia: on scoring thresholds we saw that lowering the reranker threshold reduced false positives but also lowered recall for the 'policy compliance' tag. can we tune per-intent?
[07:12] Jonah: yes per-intent thresholds are supported; you can configure route-level thresholds in the console. we recommend intent buckets with at least 500 samples to avoid noisy thresholds.
[07:22] Amir: security again: do threshold changes get audited as config changes? we need that for SOC2 evidence.
[07:27] Lina: yes, config changes are versioned and logged with operator identity and timestamp, and we can export that for audits.
[07:33] [08:00] Maya: ok let's talk fallback behavior. last failover we saw fallback to a smaller model but the output style changed and broke a downstream parser. how do we mitigate style drift on fallback?
[08:12] Jonah: good point. we have a style-preserve adapter that rewrites prompts for small-variant fallback to emulate tone and slot formatting. it's not perfect but reduces parser breakage. we can also do post-processing normalization in your pipeline.
[08:25] Derek: can we get a sample adapter config?
[08:28] Jonah: I'll include the adapter snippet in the runbook.
[08:30] [09:00] Maya: quick check — does the adapter add latency?
[09:04] Jonah: marginal, maybe +15ms median, depends on complexity.
[09:08] [10:00] Sofia: about the regression in the financial slice, any chance it's tokenizer mismatch? we've seen that before with currency symbols.
[10:12] Jonah: yes tokenization is a suspect. we'll run a tokenization diff across the failing inputs between int8 and fp16 and flag changes.
[10:20] [11:00] Derek: can you also log KV cache hit rates correlated with accuracy per request id? we want to see hit/miss impact on regression.
[11:08] Jonah: we can surface that; we'll add a column in the bench sheet for KV hit-rate.
[11:13] [12:00] Amir: on the compliance doc: when you say audit logs can be sent to our collector, is that over a persistent TLS tunnel or via S3 export? which is preferred?
[12:22] Lina: both supported. for high-sensitivity we recommend direct syslog/TLS to your collector with mTLS. S3 exports are for bulk archival.
[12:34] [13:00] Maya: ok time check, 23 minutes left. next: experimental prompt-batching. we tried packing three user turns into a single request to reduce tokens; results looked mixed — latency improved but more semantically incorrect replies.
[13:18] Jonah: right packing reduces round-trip overhead but increases context interference. prefix/KV caching helps but only if prompts share prefixes. packing unrelated intents hurts.
[13:30] Sofia: do you have a rule-of-thumb for packing?
[13:33] Jonah: pack only same-intent sequences and keep total tokens under 1k for the int8 path. for multi-intent, keep separate requests.
[13:43] [15:00] Derek: billing/price question — does packing affect token-costs?
[15:05] Maya: it can reduce cost per logical user-turn by amortizing static tokens, but it may increase compute if you trigger the heavier kernel. we'll provide a cost-model example in the sheet.
[15:16] [16:00] Sofia: quick note, we noticed ModelCloud does an auto-prune and claims lower latency; are you aware of their approach?
[16:24] Maya: yes, they focus on heavy pruning and bespoke kernels but often sacrifice recall. worth benchmarking but watch for label shift.
[16:34] [17:00] Jonah: ok wrapping to explicit next steps: I'll run the overnight int8 vs fp16 stress with the guardrail adversarial set, toggle prefix-cache on/off, and post results.
[17:12] Maya: I'll send the pricing/quantization guide and attach the benchmark sheet and SOC2/KMS notes.
[17:18] Derek: we'll prep the 10k anonymized prompt slice and share by Friday.
[17:22] Amir: i'll follow up about the audit log format and confirm KMS requirements.
[17:26] Maya: scheduling — let's pencil a 30-minute runbook+fallback deep-dive on Tuesday 2027-08-24 09:00 PT.
[17:33] Eve: works for us.
[17:35] [19:00] Maya: any final questions?
[19:03] Sofia: none, thanks.
[19:06] Maya: cool thanks everyone. we'll follow up in the thread with the sheet link and runbook draft.

References shared in chat: https://redwood.storage/benchmarks/kestrel-2027-08-18 (benchmark sheet), https://redwood.docs/runbooks/fallback-sample (runbook draft), security attachments: SOC2-scope.pdf

Transcript notes: some names and product terms auto-transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache, "redwood 13 beta" instead of redwood-13b). occasional crosstalk and interrupted phrases.

End of transcript.
